title: Coastal Wetland Restoration and Greenhouse Gas Pathways: A Global Meta‐Analysis
content:
Using 351 paired comparisons from 82 field studies, we found coastal wetland restoration increased plant biomass and soil carbon, but we detected no change in CO2, CH4, or N2O fluxes. Evidence was biased toward mangroves and (sub)tropical Asia, and gas data were scarce, so the net climate benefit remains unquantified.


ABSTRACT

Coastal wetland restoration is widely promoted as a tool for climate change mitigation, but its effect on the carbon cycle is not well constrained. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of peer-reviewed field studies that directly contrasted restored with altered sites, covering carbon stocks and greenhouse gas fluxes across mangroves, saltmarshes, seagrass meadows, brackish systems, and coastal freshwater wetlands. We analyzed 351 pairwise restored versus altered site comparisons from 82 studies. Here we show that restoration increases aboveground and belowground biomass on average, primarily through vegetation establishment at previously unvegetated sites. Soil carbon also increased, both as concentration and as areal stock (sampling depths 2–300 cm), although this effect was not detectable when analyses were restricted to samples from the upper 30 cm. No detectable changes in CO2, CH4, and N2O fluxes (33, 31, and 20 comparisons) were observed, although the available data had the power to detect only large effects. Meta-regressions detected no significant differences among wetland types, though this result is constrained by unbalanced evidence across systems and studied parameters. The available data are geographically biased toward tropical and subtropical Asia, with minimal coverage in Africa and limited data from temperate and cold coastal regions. Dissolved organic carbon was too rarely reported to be analyzed (nine comparisons from two studies), constraining whole-system impact estimates. Overall, restoration increases plant biomass on average, whereas the soil carbon and greenhouse gas terms that determine its net climate benefit cannot yet be quantified from the published literature. To translate these findings into policy-ready estimates, monitoring of greenhouse gases and dissolved organic carbon should be expanded, soil carbon and gas flux measurements should be standardized, altered versus restored designs should be prioritized, and underrepresented regions and wetland types should be targeted.
